Solutions for the end-of-chapter exercises in Chapter 3 — Data Wrangling. Datasets: olympic_athletes and medal_table from olympicAthletes, and episodes from steves — a tidied snapshot of every Rick Steves’ Europe episode (159 rows × 38 columns).

A note on coverage. Sections 3.8.2 (relocate) and 3.8.3 (rename) are short (≈10–15 lines each) — both verbs are trivial reorderings of an existing data frame, so a single combined exercise (EX3.31) exercises them alongside select() rather than padding three near-duplicate prompts. The pipe operator (3.1) is implicitly practiced in every other exercise; EX3.4 makes the nested-vs-piped equivalence explicit.

Difficulty stars on each exercise: ★ warm-up, ★★ standard application, ★★★ critical thinking.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(olympicAthletes)
library(steves)

NoteEX3.2 — show question

EX3.2 (★) Predict, then verify: what is the range of imdb_rating in episodes? What is the range of season?

Solution (reference: Chapter 2 overview, exploring data).

IMDB ratings span ~7 to ~9 (the show is well-loved). Seasons run 1–13.

range(episodes$imdb_rating, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 6.4 9.2
range(episodes$season)
[1]  1 13
NoteEX3.3 — show question

EX3.3 (★) original_air_date has type Date. Why does that matter for arithmetic (e.g., computing days between episodes) compared to storing the same as character?

Solution (reference: Section 3.5 “mutate existing variables”, date arithmetic).

With Date, you can compute differences directly (date2 - date1 returns days) and arrange() chronologically without lexicographic surprises. Strings would need to be parsed every time you wanted to do anything date-aware.

The pipe operator |>

NoteEX3.4 — show question

EX3.4 (★) Take this nested expression and rewrite it as a |>-piped chain. Verify the two produce identical output.

head(filter(olympic_athletes, year == 2024, !is.na(height)), 10)

In one sentence, why does the piped version usually read more naturally for humans than the nested one?

Solution (reference: Section 3.1 “The pipe operator |>”).

The two forms are equivalent. The pipe reads left-to-right, top-to-bottom — the same direction English readers move through text — whereas the nested form reads inside-out (innermost call first). For three or more steps the pipe wins decisively.

The piped chain also makes it trivial to add or remove a step (just insert/delete a |> verb() line); editing the nested form requires wrangling parentheses.

filter()

NoteEX3.5 — show question

EX3.5 (★) Filter olympic_athletes to athletes from sport == "Swimming" who won a Gold medal. How many rows result?

Solution (reference: Section 3.2 “filter rows”).

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(sport == "Swimming", medal == "Gold") |>
  nrow()
[1] 1159
NoteEX3.6 — show question

EX3.6 (★) Filter episodes to those where primary_country == "Italy". How many Italy episodes does the show have?

Solution (reference: Section 3.2 “filter rows”).

episodes |> filter(primary_country == "Italy") |> nrow()
[1] 29

Italy is the most-visited single country (~29 episodes).

NoteEX3.7 — show question

EX3.7 (★) Filter episodes to highly-rated AND well-watched episodes: imdb_rating >= 8 AND imdb_votes >= 50.

Solution (reference: Section 3.2 “filter rows”, boolean operators).

episodes |>
  filter(imdb_rating >= 8, imdb_votes >= 50) |>
  select(season, episode_in_season, title, imdb_rating, imdb_votes)
# A tibble: 0 × 5
# ℹ 5 variables: season <int>, episode_in_season <int>, title <chr>,
#   imdb_rating <dbl>, imdb_votes <int>
NoteEX3.8 — show question

EX3.8 (★) Filter episodes to the union: episodes about "Italy" OR "France". Use %in%.

Solution (reference: Section 3.2 “filter rows”, `%in%).

episodes |>
  filter(primary_country %in% c("Italy", "France")) |>
  count(primary_country)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  primary_country     n
  <chr>           <int>
1 France             15
2 Italy              29
NoteEX3.9 — show question

EX3.9 (★★) Filter olympic_athletes to the most recent Summer Games (year == 2024 & season == "Summer"). How many distinct athletes participated?

Solution (reference: Section 3.2 “filter rows”).

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(year == 2024, season == "Summer") |>
  summarize(n_distinct_athletes = n_distinct(id))
  n_distinct_athletes
1               10835

group_by() + summarize()

NoteEX3.10 — show question

EX3.10 (★★) Compute the mean height per sport (drop NAs with na.rm = TRUE). Show the 10 sports with the tallest mean.

Solution (reference: Section 3.4 “group_by rows” + 3.3 “summarize variables”).

olympic_athletes |>
  group_by(sport) |>
  summarize(mean_height = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(mean_height, n = 10)

EX3.13 (★★) Count the number of episodes per season of Rick Steves’ Europe. Plot it as a barplot.

Solution (reference: Section 3.4 “group_by rows” + Section 2.8 “Barplots”).

episodes |>
  count(season) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(season), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "season", y = "Number of episodes")

NoteEX3.15 — show question

EX3.15 (★★★) Compute mean age per sport, but only for sports with at least 1,000 athlete-rows. Why is the second filter important?

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize variables”, `n().

The post-summary filter keeps the comparison meaningful — averages computed on tiny samples are noisy.

olympic_athletes |>
  group_by(sport) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 1000) |>
  arrange(mean_age) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  sport                     n mean_age
  <chr>                 <int>    <dbl>
1 Swimming              26388     20.8
2 Figure Skating         3004     22.2
3 Synchronized Swimming  1149     22.4
4 Diving                 3129     22.6
5 Gymnastics            29413     22.6
NoteEX3.16 — show question

EX3.16 (★★) For each games, count the number of distinct events. Has the number of events grown over time? Plot it.

Solution (reference: Section 3.4 “group_by rows”).

Yes, the long-run trend is upward (more disciplines, more events per discipline).

olympic_athletes |>
  group_by(year, season) |>
  summarize(n_events = n_distinct(event), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_events, color = season)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Distinct events")

mutate()

NoteEX3.17 — show question

EX3.17 (★★) Add a height_in column to olympic_athletes: convert height (cm) to inches (1 inch ≈ 2.54 cm).

Solution (reference: Section 3.5 “mutate existing variables”).

olympic_athletes |>
  mutate(height_in = height / 2.54) |>
  select(name, height, height_in) |>
  head()
                        name height height_in
1       Arthur Charles Blake     NA        NA
2             Angelos Fetsis     NA        NA
3 Edwin Harold "Teddy" Flack     NA        NA
4                 Carl Galle    154  60.62992
5       Dimitrios P. Golemis     NA        NA
6  Konstantinos Karakatsanis     NA        NA
NoteEX3.18 — show question

EX3.18 (★★) Add a bmi column to olympic_athletes computed from weight (kg) and height (cm) as weight / (height / 100)^2. Show the first few rows where bmi is non-missing.

Solution (reference: Section 3.5 “mutate existing variables”, arithmetic across columns).

olympic_athletes |>
  mutate(bmi = weight / (height / 100)^2) |>
  filter(!is.na(bmi)) |>
  select(name, sport, height, weight, bmi) |>
  head()
                        name     sport height weight      bmi
1                 Carl Galle Athletics    154     45 18.97453
2  Thomas Edmund "Tom" Burke Athletics    183     66 19.70796
3 Thomas Pelham "Tom" Curtis Athletics    176     66 21.30682
4        Kurt Wilhelm Doerry Athletics    179     73 22.78331
5          Launceston Elliot Athletics    188    102 28.85921
6              Fritz Hofmann Athletics    167     56 20.07960

mutate() is happy to compute new columns from arithmetic combinations of multiple existing columns. The / 100 converts height from centimeters to meters first; squaring gives meters² in the denominator, which matches the standard BMI definition (kg/m²).

NoteEX3.19 — show question

EX3.19 (★★) Add a logical column won_medal to olympic_athletes that is TRUE for any non-missing medal. What proportion of athlete-rows won a medal?

Solution (reference: Section 3.5 “mutate existing variables”, boolean coercion).

olympic_athletes |>
  mutate(won_medal = !is.na(medal)) |>
  summarize(pct_with_medal = mean(won_medal))
  pct_with_medal
1      0.1399537

About 14% of athlete-rows are part of a medal-winning entry. (Team events count each roster member.)

join()

NoteEX3.24 — show question

EX3.24 (★★★) editions (5 rows) has metadata for the 2018–2026 Games. Use inner_join() to attach editions to olympic_athletes. What is the resulting row count? Why didn’t it equal the original 314,749?

Solution (reference: Section 3.7 “join data frames”, inner_join).

editions only covers 2018–2026, so an inner join keeps only athletes from those Games. The original 314,749 rows shrink to the count of athletes in those 5 Games.

olympic_athletes |>
  inner_join(editions, by = c("games" = "games")) |>
  nrow()
Warning in inner_join(olympic_athletes, editions, by = c(games = "games")): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 55611 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.
[1] 320217
NoteEX3.25 — show question

EX3.25 (★★★) Use left_join() instead. What’s the row count, and why is it different from the inner-join result?

Solution (reference: Section 3.7 “join data frames”, left_join).

left_join preserves all athlete rows; rows whose games value isn’t in editions get NAs for the joined columns. So the count matches the original 314,749.

olympic_athletes |>
  left_join(editions, by = c("games" = "games")) |>
  nrow()
Warning in left_join(olympic_athletes, editions, by = c(games = "games")): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 55611 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.
[1] 320217

EX3.26 (★★★) Use anti_join() between olympic_athletes and medal_table (joining on year/year and noc/noc) to find athletes whose NOC did not appear in medal_table for that Games. What does this tell you about coverage?

Solution (reference: Section 3.7 “join data frames”, anti_join + filtering joins).

These are NOCs that participated but won no medals at that Games — the bulk of NOCs in any given Olympics.

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(year >= 2018) |>
  anti_join(medal_table, by = c("year" = "year", "noc" = "noc")) |>
  count(year, season, noc, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

5  2018 Winter NAN 1081
6  2024 Summer NGR   82
7  2026 Winter UKR   79
8  2022 Winter DEN   69
9  2022 Winter KAZ   68
10 2026 Winter SVK   67
NoteEX3.27 — show question

EX3.27 (★★★) Use semi_join() to keep only the athletes from countries that appear in medal_table (i.e., medal-winning countries from 2018–2026). How many rows remain?

Solution (reference: Section 3.7 “join data frames”, semi_join).

semi_join() filters x rows to those that match y — without bringing along y’s columns.

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(year >= 2018) |>
  semi_join(medal_table, by = c("year" = "year", "noc" = "noc")) |>
  nrow()
[1] 30385

NoteEX3.31 — show question

EX3.31 (★★) Build a small wrangling pipeline on medal_table that uses three of the Other verbs from Section 3.8 — select(), relocate(), and rename(). Goal: keep only the columns noc, country, gold, silver, bronze, total; rename noc to iso_code; reorder columns so country comes first. Show the first 5 rows of the result.

Solution (reference: Section 3.8 “Other verbs”, select + relocate + `rename).

medal_table |>
  select(noc, country, gold, silver, bronze, total) |>
  rename(iso_code = noc) |>
  relocate(country) |>
  head(5)
        country iso_code gold silver bronze total
1 United States      USA   11      7      2    20
2        Greece      GRE   10     18     19    47
3       Germany      GER    6      5      2    13
4        France      FRA    5      4      2    11
5 Great Britain      GBR    2      3      2     7

select() keeps the columns we want (and drops the rest), rename() swaps the name of one column without moving it, and relocate() reorders columns without changing names or count. The verbs are composable — each does one job, and the pipe lets you stack them in any order. (Order does matter: if you rename() first, you must reference the new name in subsequent calls.)

Critical thinking and open exploration

NoteEX3.32 — show question

EX3.32 (★★) Run mean(olympic_athletes$height) (without na.rm). What do you get, and why?

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize variables”, `na.rm).

The result is NA — any NA in the input poisons the mean. Use na.rm = TRUE to ignore them.

mean(olympic_athletes$height)
[1] NA
mean(olympic_athletes$height, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 175.2992
NoteEX3.33 — show question

EX3.33 (★★★) Compare two coding styles for the same task: (a) save each intermediate result to a variable, (b) chain everything with |>. Pick a 3-step dplyr chain and write it both ways. Which is easier to modify? Which is easier to debug?

Solution (reference: Section 3.1 “The pipe operator |>”).

Piped style is easier to modify (insert/swap a step in one line) and easier to read top-to-bottom. Intermediate-variable style is easier to debug step-by-step (you can View(step1) between calls).

# Intermediate variables
step1 <- filter(olympic_athletes, sport == "Athletics")
step2 <- group_by(step1, year)
step3 <- summarize(step2, mean_h = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE))

# Piped (same)
olympic_athletes |>
  filter(sport == "Athletics") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(mean_h = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE))
NoteEX3.34 — show question

EX3.34 (★★★) Pick two countries (e.g., "USA" and "GBR") and produce a single linegraph of their total medals across the five recent Games. What story does the chart tell?

Solution (reference: Sections 3.4 “group_by rows” + 2.4 “Linegraphs”).

medal_table |>
  filter(noc %in% c("USA", "GBR")) |>
  group_by(noc, year) |>
  summarize(total = sum(total), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total, color = noc)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Total medals (Summer + Winter)")
NoteEX3.35 — show question

EX3.35 (★★★) From episodes, compute episodes per primary_country and identify the most-featured country. Then compute the same with geo_match == "full" (only fully geo-resolved episodes) — does the leader change?

Solution (reference: Section 3.2 “filter rows” + 3.4 “group_by rows”).

Italy is typically the leader in both — the geo-match filter mostly removes “compilation” or multi-country episodes (geo_match == "country" etc.).

episodes |> count(primary_country, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 5)
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  primary_country     n
  <chr>           <int>
1 Italy              29
2 Multiple           20
3 United Kingdom     20
4 France             15
5 Germany             9
episodes |>
  filter(geo_match == "full") |>
  count(primary_country, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 5)
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  primary_country     n
  <chr>           <int>
1 Italy              23
2 United Kingdom     19
3 France             13
4 Spain               7
5 Turkey              5
NoteEX3.36 — show question

EX3.36 (★★★) Construct a “country diversity” metric per Games: for each year/season, count the number of distinct nocs in olympic_athletes. Plot the trend over time. Has the Olympics become more globally inclusive?

Solution (reference: Section 3.4 “group_by rows”, time-series summary).

The Olympic movement has expanded substantially since 1896.

olympic_athletes |>
  group_by(year, season) |>
  summarize(n_nocs = n_distinct(noc), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_nocs, color = season)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Distinct NOCs")
NoteEX3.37 — show question

EX3.37 (★★★) Open exploration: combining at least two dplyr verbs and one of the two datasets, find one finding that surprises you. State your finding in one sentence above the supporting code.

Solution (reference: Chapter 3 — synthesis).

Answers will vary. Example: “Among Rick Steves' Europe episodes, British Isles episodes have the highest median IMDB rating among regions with at least 10 episodes.”

episodes |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarize(n = n(), median_rating = median(imdb_rating, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(median_rating))
# A tibble: 7 × 3
  region             n median_rating
  <chr>          <int>         <dbl>
1 British Isles     23          8   
2 Multi-Region      20          8   
3 Western Europe    26          7.8 
4 Eastern Europe    10          7.65
5 Beyond Europe     13          7.6 
6 Mediterranean     34          7.6 
7 Iberia            13          7.4

Ch 2 visualizations that needed Ch 3 wrangling first (deferred from Ch 2)

NoteEX3.38 — show question

EX3.38 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — a missingness summary requires summarize() + is.na() from this chapter.

height and weight in olympic_athletes have many NA values, especially for older Games. Predict — without running code — why this is. Then use summarize() and mean(is.na(...)) to compute the proportion of NAs in each of those two columns.

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize rows”, is.na()).

Bio data was not systematically reported in early-20th-century Games; coverage improved over time but is still incomplete for the most recent Games (privacy / late data ingest). The proportion of NAs for height/weight is roughly 30–35 % overall.

olympic_athletes |>
  summarize(
    pct_height_na = mean(is.na(height)),
    pct_weight_na = mean(is.na(weight))
  )
  pct_height_na pct_weight_na
1      0.274658     0.2886096
NoteEX3.39 — show question

EX3.39 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — the linegraph* is Ch 2’s geom (§ 2.4), but computing a row’s total_medals = gold + silver + bronze requires mutate() from § 3.5.*

Using medal_table, plot the total medals (gold + silver + bronze) won by "USA" across the five recent Games as a linegraph (year on the x-axis). You’ll need filter() → mutate() → ggplot().

Solution (reference: Section 3.5 “mutate existing variables” + Ch 2 § 2.4 linegraphs).

A note on style — piping wrangled data straight into ggplot(). Ch 3 § 3.1 noted that |> chains data-wrangling steps the way + chains ggplot layers. You can join the two: pipe your wrangled data into ggplot(), then keep adding layers with +. Two equivalent forms — the chained version is shorter; the temp-data-frame version is easier to debug and lets you reuse the data frame for other plots.

Chained form:

medal_table |>
  filter(noc == "USA") |>
  mutate(total_medals = gold + silver + bronze) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total_medals)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "games (year)", y = "Total medals (USA)")

Temp-data-frame form (same plot, two-step):

usa_medals <- medal_table |>
  filter(noc == "USA") |>
  mutate(total_medals = gold + silver + bronze)
ggplot(usa_medals, aes(x = year, y = total_medals)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "games (year)", y = "Total medals (USA)")
NoteEX3.40 — show question

EX3.40 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — linegraph from § 2.4, but counting distinct athletes per Games needs group_by() + summarize(n_distinct(...)) from §§ 3.3–3.4.

Compute the number of distinct athletes per Games in olympic_athletes and plot it as a linegraph against year. Filter to a single season (Summer or Winter) — combining them would mix two cycles.

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize” + 3.4 “group_by” + Ch 2 § 2.4 linegraphs).

Linegraphs require a single ordered sequence on the x-axis — Summer and Winter alternate every 2 years and would zig-zag if mixed.

Temp-data-frame form:

summer_athletes <- olympic_athletes |>
  filter(season == "Summer") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(n_athletes = n_distinct(id), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(summer_athletes, aes(x = year, y = n_athletes)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Distinct athletes (Summer games)")

Chained form (equivalent):

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(season == "Summer") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(n_athletes = n_distinct(id), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_athletes)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Distinct athletes (Summer games)")
NoteEX3.41 — show question

EX3.41 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — linegraph from § 2.4, but the per-year, per-sport mean(height) needs group_by() + summarize().

For one sport of your choice, plot mean height per year over time. Has the typical height of athletes in that sport grown, shrunk, or stayed flat?

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize” + 3.4 “group_by” + Ch 2 § 2.4 linegraphs).

Answers will vary by sport. Basketball trends upward — average height has grown ~10 cm over the past century.

Temp-data-frame form:

basketball_height <- olympic_athletes |>
  filter(sport == "Basketball") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(mean_height = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(basketball_height, aes(x = year, y = mean_height)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Mean height (cm)", title = "Olympic basketball: rising stature")

From here on, solutions in this group use the chained form by default — feel free to refactor any of them into a temp-data-frame form if it helps you debug.

NoteEX3.42 — show question

EX3.42 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — facets are Ch 2 material (§ 2.6), but identifying the top-5 NOCs first requires group_by() + summarize() + slicing.

Filter to the top-5 NOCs in medal_table (by total medals across all Games), then use facet_wrap(~ noc) to show a geom_col barplot of medal totals per Games for each NOC.

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize” + 3.4 “group_by” + Ch 2 § 2.6 facets).

top5_noc <- medal_table |>
  group_by(noc) |> summarize(t = sum(total), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(t, n = 5) |> pull(noc)

medal_table |>
  filter(noc %in% top5_noc) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total, fill = season)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ noc, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "year", y = "Total medals", fill = "season")
NoteEX3.43 — show question

EX3.43 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — boxplots are Ch 2 material (§ 2.7), but identifying the top-5 sports first requires group_by() + summarize() + top_n().

Identify the 5 sports with the most athletes by group_by(sport), summarize(n_athletes = n()), then top_n(n = 5, wt = n_athletes). Build boxplots of height for just those five sports. Which sport has the highest median height? Which has the largest IQR?

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize” + 3.4 “group_by” + 3.8.4 top_n() + Ch 2 § 2.7 boxplots).

top5_sports <- olympic_athletes |>
  group_by(sport) |>
  summarize(n_athletes = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  top_n(n = 5, wt = n_athletes) |>
  pull(sport)

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(sport %in% top5_sports) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sport, y = height)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()
NoteEX3.44 — show question

EX3.44 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — bar chart geom is Ch 2 (§ 2.8.1), but computing the top-10 NOCs across all Games needs group_by() + summarize() + slicing.

Use medal_table to find the 10 NOCs with the most total medals across all five recent Games combined. Display them as a horizontal bar chart, sorted descending.

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 “summarize” + 3.4 “group_by” + Ch 2 § 2.8 barplots).

top10 <- medal_table |>
  group_by(noc, country) |>
  summarize(total = sum(total), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10)

ggplot(top10, aes(x = total, y = reorder(country, total))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Total medals (2018–2026)", y = NULL)
NoteEX3.45 — show question

EX3.45 (★★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — stacked bars are Ch 2 (§ 2.8.3), but turning the wide gold/silver/bronze columns into a medal_type column requires pivot_longer() from Ch 4.

Modify your top-10 plot (from EX 3.44) to stack gold/silver/bronze in each bar. Hint: pivot_longer() first, then map fill = medal_type.

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 + 3.4 + pivot_longer() from Ch 4 + Ch 2 § 2.8.3).

Two new things show up in this solution: pivot_longer() (from tidyr, previewed here from Ch 4) and the stacked bar from Ch 2 § 2.8.3.

library(tidyr)
top10 <- medal_table |>
  group_by(noc, country) |>
  summarize(
    gold   = sum(gold),
    silver = sum(silver),
    bronze = sum(bronze),
    total  = sum(total),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10)

top10 |>
  pivot_longer(c(gold, silver, bronze),
               names_to = "medal_type", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(medal_type = factor(medal_type, levels = c("bronze", "silver", "gold"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(country, n, sum), fill = medal_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Medals (2018–2026)", y = NULL, fill = "medal")

Notice how we wrote one sum(...) line per medal-type column inside summarize(). This is the Ch 3 style: name each new column explicitly. (dplyr has a helper called across() that lets you write summarize(across(c(gold, silver, bronze), sum), ...) for the same result — it’s worth knowing once you reach for it, but it’s not introduced in this chapter.)

NoteEX3.46 — show question

EX3.46 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — bars are Ch 2 (§ 2.8.1), but ranking the top 10 NOCs at a single Games needs filter() + top_n() from this chapter.

Build a barplot of medal counts for the 2024 Summer Games only (one bar per top-10 NOC, using top_n()). What’s the top NOC?

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 + 3.4 + Ch 2 § 2.8 barplots).

The U.S. is typically the top NOC for the 2024 Summer Games.

medal_table |>
  filter(games == "2024 Summer") |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total, y = reorder(country, total))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Total medals", y = NULL, title = "2024 Summer — top 10 NOCs")
NoteEX3.47 — show question

EX3.47 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — dodged bars are Ch 2 (§ 2.8.3), but identifying the top-5 NOCs by total medals requires group_by() + summarize() + slicing.

Using medal_table and the top-5 NOCs by total medals, build a dodged (side-by-side) barplot of medal counts split by season — three bars per NOC, color-filled by season. Hint: summarize by noc and season, then geom_col(position = "dodge").

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 + 3.4 + Ch 2 § 2.8.3 dodged bars).

Dodging puts the Summer/Winter bars next to each other inside each NOC group, so the eye can compare seasons within a country at a glance. For most top-5 NOCs the Summer bar dominates Winter — except for traditional winter powers (e.g., NOR), where the dodged view makes the season skew unmistakable.

top5 <- medal_table |>
  group_by(noc) |> summarize(t = sum(total), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(t, n = 5) |> pull(noc)

medal_table |>
  filter(noc %in% top5) |>
  group_by(noc, season) |>
  summarize(total = sum(total), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total, y = reorder(noc, total), fill = season)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Medals (2018–2026)", y = NULL, fill = "season")
NoteEX3.48 — show question

EX3.48 (★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — position = "fill" bars are Ch 2 (§ 2.8.3), but reshaping the medal columns requires pivot_longer() from Ch 4.

Take the stacked gold/silver/bronze barplot from EX 3.45 and rebuild it with position = "fill" so each NOC’s bar reaches 100 %. Compare the two charts: what new question does the proportional version answer (that the stacked-counts version cannot), and conversely what does the original show that gets hidden when you switch to proportions?

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 + 3.4 + pivot_longer() from Ch 4 + Ch 2 § 2.8.3).

Same wrangling as EX 3.45 — one explicit sum(...) per medal column — but switch the bar geom to position = "fill".

library(tidyr)
top10 <- medal_table |>
  group_by(noc, country) |>
  summarize(
    gold   = sum(gold),
    silver = sum(silver),
    bronze = sum(bronze),
    total  = sum(total),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10)

top10 |>
  pivot_longer(c(gold, silver, bronze),
               names_to = "medal_type", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(medal_type = factor(medal_type,
                             levels = c("bronze", "silver", "gold"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(country, n, sum), fill = medal_type)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of medals (within noc)", y = NULL, fill = "medal")

What the proportional version answers (and the original cannot): of the medals each NOC won, what share were gold vs. silver vs. bronze? All bars now reach 100 %, so countries with very different totals can still be compared on medal mix.

What the original showed (and the proportional version hides): the absolute size of each NOC’s haul. After position = "fill", a tiny-medal-count NOC and a huge-medal-count NOC look identical — the chart no longer tells you who’s winning the medal table.

The choice is task-specific: counts answer “who won the most?”, proportions answer “who relies on golds vs. bronzes?”.

NoteEX3.49 — show question

EX3.49 (★★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — the idea* (a chart over time, colored by sex) is Ch 2 (§ 2.4), but counting distinct athletes per year × sex needs group_by() + summarize(n_distinct()).*

Build a chart that visualizes the rise of female participation in the Summer Olympics over time. (Hint: count distinct athletes per year × sex, filter to Summer.) State your finding in one sentence above the chart.

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 + 3.4 + Ch 2 § 2.4 linegraphs).

The female line rises sharply from near zero in 1900 to roughly parity with the male line by the 2020s.

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(season == "Summer") |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarize(n_athletes = n_distinct(id), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_athletes, color = sex)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(y = "Distinct athletes (Summer games)",
       title = "Women's participation has caught up to men's")
NoteEX3.50 — show question

EX3.50 (★★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — barplot is Ch 2 (§ 2.8), but counting NAs across columns needs summarize(across()) + pivot_longer() to reshape into a plottable frame.

Chapter 2 didn’t show NA visualization. Build a barplot showing the count of NAs per column in olympic_athletes. Which columns have the most missingness? Why might that be?

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 + pivot_longer() from Ch 4 + Ch 2 § 2.8 barplots).

height, weight, age, and medal are the columns with substantial missingness — older Games and recent privacy practices both contribute.

Approach 1 — Ch 3 verbs only. From glimpse(olympic_athletes) we know there are 15 columns; the ones we suspect have NAs are age, height, weight, and medal. Compute their NA counts explicitly with one summarize() argument per column:

library(tidyr)
na_counts <- olympic_athletes |>
  summarize(
    age    = sum(is.na(age)),
    height = sum(is.na(height)),
    weight = sum(is.na(weight)),
    medal  = sum(is.na(medal))
  )

na_counts |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "n_na") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_na, y = reorder(column, n_na))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "# of NAs", y = NULL)

The explicit form is honest but tedious — easy to forget a column or miscount NAs in one you didn’t think to check.

Approach 2 — across() (a dplyr helper not introduced in this chapter). When you find yourself writing the same transformation in summarize() for many columns, across() lets you do all of them at once. The pattern is across(<columns>, <function>). Here everything() selects all columns and ~ sum(is.na(.x)) is a one-line function that counts NAs in column .x.

olympic_athletes |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "n_na") |>
  filter(n_na > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_na, y = reorder(column, n_na))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "# of NAs", y = NULL)

This second version produces the same chart but checks every column — and surfaces missingness in columns you might not have suspected. Once you’re comfortable with the named-columns form, reach for across() whenever you’d otherwise be repeating the same summarize() step for many columns.

NoteEX3.51 — show question

EX3.51 (★★★) Carried over from Chapter 2 — open-ended chart-building over time is Ch 2 (§ 2.4), but the per-year per-sport mean(height) needs group_by() + summarize(), and filtering small-sample years requires a second filter() after the summary.

Pick a sport whose athletes’ average height has clearly changed over time (e.g., basketball, swimming, gymnastics). Build a chart that supports the change. Acknowledge any caveats — e.g., missing height data for older Games (use the post-summary filter() to drop years with too few observations to trust).

Solution (reference: Section 3.3 + 3.4 + Ch 2 § 2.4 linegraphs, open-ended).

Answers will vary. Volleyball average heights have climbed steadily. The post-summary filter(n > 20) is the key honesty step — it drops years where the mean was computed from only a handful of athletes, which would otherwise produce wild swings in the early decades.

olympic_athletes |>
  filter(sport == "Volleyball") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(
    mean_height = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_obs       = sum(!is.na(height)),
    .groups     = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_obs > 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_height)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Mean height (cm)",
       title = "Volleyball: athletes are getting taller")

Notice the two-step use of filter(): once before group_by() to focus on one sport, then again after summarize() to drop low-sample years. The post-summary filter() is what acknowledges the missingness caveat that the prompt asks for.

Extensions

NoteAbout these Extensions

The exercises below deliberately introduce functions and concepts beyond what this chapter teaches — log transformations, predict(), new packages, foreshadowing later chapters. They are optional, aimed at readers who want to push further. The main Exercises and Quick checks above stick strictly to what this chapter covers.

NoteEX3.52 — show question

EX3.52 (◆◆) case_when() for multi-level conditional mutates. When you want to derive a new categorical column from a numeric one with more than two buckets, case_when() is cleaner than nesting ifelse()s. Build an age_group column on olympic_athletes with buckets "under 20", "20s", "30s", "40+", then count athletes in each.

Solution (reference: Extension: case_when).

olympic_athletes |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    age < 20 ~ "under 20",
    age < 30 ~ "20s",
    age < 40 ~ "30s",
    TRUE     ~ "40+"
  )) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop")
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  age_group      n
  <chr>      <int>
1 20s       199855
2 30s        49125
3 40+        30863
4 under 20   35247

case_when() evaluates conditions in order — the first matching branch wins. The catch-all TRUE ~ ... handles everything not matched above. Reads like an English decision tree, which scales better than nested if_else()s.

NoteEX3.53 — show question

EX3.53 (◆◆) if_else() for boolean conditional mutates. When the condition has exactly two outcomes, if_else(condition, value_if_TRUE, value_if_FALSE) is the cleanest tool. It’s strict about both branches having the same type, which catches subtle bugs that base R’s ifelse() silently lets through. Try building an is_medalist column on olympic_athletes ("yes" if medal is not NA, "no" otherwise) — then count how many athlete-rows are in each.

Solution (reference: Extension: if_else).

olympic_athletes |>
  mutate(is_medalist = if_else(!is.na(medal), "yes", "no")) |>
  group_by(is_medalist) |>
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop")
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  is_medalist      n
  <chr>        <int>
1 no          270992
2 yes          44098

if_else() is strict about type matching: passing if_else(cond, "yes", FALSE) would error because the two branches return different types. Base R’s ifelse() silently coerces in that case, which can let subtle bugs through. Prefer if_else() for that reason.

NoteEX3.54 — show question

EX3.54 (◆◆) The slice_*() family. Section 3.6 introduced top_n(); the dplyr ecosystem now favors a family of slice_*() verbs that read more clearly and have explicit variants. slice_max(col, n)/slice_min(col, n) for top/bottom by a column, slice_head(n)/slice_tail(n) for first/last rows, slice_sample(n) for a random subset. Try each above. For “top 10 NOCs by medals at Paris 2024,” which would you reach for first?

Solution (reference: Extension: slice_ family)*.

# For "top 10 NOCs by medals at Paris 2024", slice_max() reads most directly:
medal_table |>
  filter(games == "2024 Summer") |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10)
   edition_id       games year season noc                    country gold
1          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer USA              United States   40
2          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer CHN People's Republic of China   40
3          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer GBR              Great Britain   14
4          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer FRA                     France   16
5          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer AUS                  Australia   18
6          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer JPN                      Japan   20
7          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer ITA                      Italy   12
8          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer NED                Netherlands   15
9          63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer GER                    Germany   12
10         63 2024 Summer 2024 Summer KOR          Republic of Korea   13
   silver bronze total notes
1      44     42   126      
2      27     24    91      
3      22     29    65      
4      26     22    64      
5      19     16    53      
6      12     13    45      
7      13     15    40      
8       7     12    34      
9      13      8    33      
10      9     10    32

slice_max() is purpose-built for “top N by value” — easier to read than arrange(desc(col)) |> head(n) or the older top_n(n, wt = col). slice_head() ignores values and just takes the first N rows as-is. slice_sample() is the dplyr equivalent of base R’s sample() on rows. Choose by intent: top by value (slice_max), positional (slice_head/slice_tail), random (slice_sample).

NoteEX3.55 — show question

EX3.55 (◆◆) count() as a summarize(n = n()) shortcut. The pattern group_by(col) |> summarize(n = n()) |> arrange(desc(n)) is so common dplyr provides count(col, sort = TRUE) as a one-liner. Use it on olympic_athletes to find the 5 most-represented sports. When you need more than one summary stat per group (e.g., mean and SD), stick with group_by() + summarize(); for pure row counts, count() wins.

Solution (reference: Extension: count() shortcut).

olympic_athletes |> count(sport, sort = TRUE) |> head(5)
       sport     n
1  Athletics 43062
2 Gymnastics 29413
3   Swimming 26388
4   Shooting 12580
5    Cycling 12358

count(sport, sort = TRUE) is shorthand for group_by(sport) |> summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(desc(n)). Use it whenever the only summary you need is row counts. For multi-stat summaries (e.g., mean and SD per group), the explicit group_by()/summarize() is still required.

NoteEX3.56 — show question

EX3.56 (◆◆◆) across() for applying a function to many columns. Writing summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), mean_height = ..., mean_weight = ...) for many columns is tedious. across(<cols>, <fn>) applies the same function to multiple columns at once. The snippet above computes mean and SD for age, height, weight all in one summarize. (We mentioned this in passing in EX 3.50 — here’s the dedicated walk-through.)

Solution (reference: Extension: across()).

olympic_athletes |>
  summarize(across(c(age, height, weight),
                   list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                        sd   = \(x) sd(x,   na.rm = TRUE))))
  age_mean   age_sd height_mean height_sd weight_mean weight_sd
1 25.59707 6.300654    175.2992  10.48933    70.61317  14.31626

across(<cols>, <fn>) applies a function to each named column. Passing a list of functions (with names) produces output columns named colname_listname, e.g., age_mean, age_sd. The \(x) ... syntax is R’s compact anonymous-function notation. The savings scale with column count: one line of across() replaces three (or thirty) lines of repeated summarize() arguments.

NoteEX3.57 — show question

EX3.57 (◆◆) bind_rows() and bind_cols(). When you have two data frames with the same columns and want to stack them vertically, use bind_rows(). For two frames with the same rows in the same order that you want to glue side-by-side, use bind_cols() (rare — usually a join is safer). Try bind_rows() to combine 2024 Summer and 2022 Winter medal tables. Why is bind_rows() safer than rbind() (the base-R equivalent)?

Solution (reference: Extension: bind_rows/bind_cols).

summer_2024 <- medal_table |> filter(games == "2024 Summer")
winter_2022 <- medal_table |> filter(games == "2022 Winter")
bind_rows(summer_2024, winter_2022)

bind_rows() matches columns by name, fills missing columns with NA, and preserves data types. Base R’s rbind() matches columns by position — so two data frames with the same columns in a different order silently get mismatched. bind_rows() is the safer default.

NoteEX3.58 — show question

EX3.58 (◆◆◆) String manipulation with stringr. Real-world data is full of text that needs cleaning. The stringr package provides a consistent family of str_*() functions: str_detect() (does the string match this pattern?), str_replace() (swap one pattern for another), str_to_lower(), str_trim(). Use the snippet above to flag team events in olympic_athletes$event. Briefly: when would you want regular expressions in the pattern argument vs. literal strings?

Solution (reference: Extension: stringr basics).

library(stringr)
olympic_athletes |>
  mutate(is_team_event = str_detect(event, "Team|Doubles|Relay")) |>
  count(is_team_event)
  is_team_event      n
1         FALSE 264380
2          TRUE  50710

Regular expressions ("Team|Doubles|Relay" — the | means “or”) are powerful when the pattern has variants you want to catch in one shot. Use literal strings (with fixed = TRUE for clarity) when the pattern is exact and contains characters with regex meaning you don’t want interpreted (e.g., ., +, ().

NoteEX3.59 — show question

EX3.59 (◆◆◆) Date handling with lubridate. Dates look like strings but behave like numbers — and parsing them by hand with substr() and as.numeric() is error-prone. The lubridate package gives you tidy parsers (ymd(), mdy(), dmy()) and extractors (year(), month(), wday()). Use it on episodes$original_air_date to add year, month, and weekday columns. Which weekday did Rick Steves’ Europe air on most often?

Solution (reference: Extension: lubridate basics).

library(lubridate)

Attaching package: 'lubridate'
The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    date, intersect, setdiff, union
episodes |>
  mutate(
    year_aired  = year(original_air_date),
    month_aired = month(original_air_date, label = TRUE),
    weekday     = wday(original_air_date, label = TRUE)
  ) |>
  count(weekday, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  weekday     n
  <ord>   <int>
1 Sun       120
2 Sat        29
3 Wed         6
4 Fri         2
5 Mon         1
6 Thu         1

Public-television shows tend to have a consistent weekly broadcast day; the counts will show one weekday dominating. lubridate::year() masks base::year — if that matters, qualify with lubridate::year(...). The label = TRUE argument gets you human-readable factor levels ("Mon", "Tue", …) instead of integers.

NoteEX3.60 — show question

EX3.60 (◆◆◆) Splitting columns with separate_wider_delim(). When one column packs two pieces of info (e.g., "2024 Summer"), tidyr::separate_wider_delim() splits it on a delimiter into named output columns. Apply it to medal_table$games. (Compare your result to medal_table’s existing year and season columns — same info, but you’ve reconstructed it from the combined string.)

Solution (reference: Extension: separate_wider_delim).

library(tidyr)
medal_table |>
  separate_wider_delim(games, delim = " ",
                       names = c("year_str", "season_split"))
# A tibble: 1,929 × 12
   edition_id year_str season_split  year season noc   country       gold silver
        <int> <chr>    <chr>        <int> <chr>  <chr> <chr>        <int>  <int>
 1          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer USA   United Stat…    11      7
 2          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer GRE   Greece          10     18
 3          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer GER   Germany          6      5
 4          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer FRA   France           5      4
 5          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer GBR   Great Brita…     2      3
 6          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer HUN   Hungary          2      1
 7          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer AUT   Austria          2      1
 8          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer AUS   Australia        2      0
 9          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer DEN   Denmark          1      2
10          1 1896     Summer        1896 Summer SUI   Switzerland      1      2
# ℹ 1,919 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: bronze <int>, total <int>, notes <chr>

The output has new columns year_str and season_split that match the existing year and season columns. Why use it when those columns already exist? Because in real datasets you often don’t — many imported files pack date and category into one string, and separate_wider_delim() is the cleanest way to undo that.

NoteEX3.61 — show question

EX3.61 (◆◆◆) rowwise() for row-by-row computation. Most dplyr verbs are vectorized (operate on whole columns at once), which is fast but awkward when you need a per-row reduction across multiple columns. rowwise() switches dplyr to per-row mode. The snippet finds, for each (Games × NOC) row, which medal color the country won the most of. Always pair rowwise() with ungroup() when you’re done — otherwise subsequent verbs stay slow.

Solution (reference: Extension: rowwise()).

medal_table |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(best_color = c("gold","silver","bronze")[which.max(c(gold, silver, bronze))]) |>
  ungroup() |>
  count(best_color, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  best_color     n
  <chr>      <int>
1 bronze       687
2 gold         650
3 silver       592

Without rowwise(), which.max(c(gold, silver, bronze)) would operate on the entire columns (giving one answer for the whole data frame, not one per row). rowwise() is essentially group_by(row) — fast enough for thousands of rows, but inefficient at millions. For row-level reductions across many columns, rowwise() + c(...) is the readable pattern; apply() and matrix operations are the fast pattern.
